newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, Irish prime minister discuss peace talks.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Irish prime minister discuss peace talks.

text.p: President Bill Clinton called Irish Prime Minister Bertie Ahern on Tuesday to congratulate him on his recent election victory and discuss the Northern Ireland peace process, the White House said.

"They had a very warm chat," White House spokesman Mike McCurry said. "They clearly reviewed the current efforts by both the Irish government and by the British government to move the Northern Ireland peace talks into a more substantive phase -- ideally with the participation of Sinn Fein based on an unequivocal ceasefire."

"But absent that at the moment, they reviewed ways in which talks at this very critical and delicate time might move forward so that the promise of peace could become real for the people of Northern Ireland," McCurry added.
McCurry said the two agreed to remain in contact and that Clinton offered to do whatever possible to be helpful to the parties in the peace process.
He said it was possible Clinton could meet Ahern, who took office last month, some time in the near future.
McCurry said Clinton met Ahern in Dublin in 1995 and the two had corresponded since Ahern took office on June 26. He said the telephone call was a "good opportunity" for them to renew contacts.

Multi-party peace talks resume in Belfast on Tuesday under a cloud of violence and a dispute over Britain's admission that it had been in contact with the Irish Republican Army's (IRA) political wing, Sinn Fein.

Britain and Ireland broke contacts with Sinn Fein after the IRA shot dead two policemen in an ambush a month ago. Northern Ireland Secretary Mo Mowlam acknowledged on Monday that officials had been in touch with Sinn Fein after the group sought clarification of the requirements for its admission to peace talks, angering Protestant Unionists.

Tension remains high in Northern Ireland after a Protestant Orange Order parade down the Catholic Garvaghy Road area of Portadown nine days ago sparked nights of violence and prompted Catholics to threaten mass counter demonstrations.

The Northern Ireland conflict pits the IRA and others who wish to end British rule of the province against Protestant Loyalists who want to remain part of Britain. Some 3,200 people have been killed in the conflict over the past three decades.
